generated_test.title: Insert a second user with a distinct email succeeds
preconditions: The users table exists with a unique, non-null email column.
The users table contains exactly one user with email alice@example.com.
setup_sql: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;
CREATE TABLE users (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO users (user_id, email) VALUES (1, 'alice@example.com');

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;
SELECT user_id, email FROM users ORDER BY user_id;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email = 'bob@example.com';

expected_outcome.assertion_description: The INSERT succeeds without error; the users table contains two rows: alice@example.com and bob@example.com.

generated_test.title: Reject insert of duplicate email into users table via UNIQUE constraint
preconditions: The users table exists with a UNIQUE constraint on the email column.
A user with email alice@example.com already exists in the users table.
constraints: The existing row for alice@example.com must remain unchanged after the rejected insert.
setup_sql: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'alice@example.com');
generated_test.test_sql: INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (2, 'Alice Duplicate', 'alice@example.com');

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;

expected_outcome.assertion_description: The INSERT fails with a UNIQUE constraint violation (duplicate key value violates unique constraint) and the existing row for alice@example.com remains unchanged; the table still contains exactly one row.

generated_test.title: Insert order referencing non-existent customer 999 fails with foreign key violation
preconditions: The customers and orders tables exist.
The orders table is initially empty.
Customer 999 does not exist in the customers table.
Foreign key enforcement is enabled (PostgreSQL always enforces foreign keys).
constraints: orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.customer_id.
Customer 999 must not exist in customers.
orders must remain empty after the rejected insert.
setup_sql: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers;
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id));
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, name) VALUES (1, 'Alice');
generated_test.test_sql: INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, amount) VALUES (1, 999, 50.00);

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 999;
SELECT customer_id, name FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;

expected_outcome.assertion_description: The INSERT into orders referencing customer 999 is rejected with a foreign key constraint violation, and the orders table remains empty.

generated_test.title: Insert of email differing only by letter case from existing user is rejected as duplicate

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;
SELECT user_id, email FROM users ORDER BY user_id;

expected_outcome.assertion_description: Inserting 'alice@example.com' when 'Alice@example.com' already exists fails with a unique violation (duplicate key value violates unique constraint), and the users table still contains only the original row.

generated_test.title: Deleting customer 1 cascade-deletes its two orders while customer 2 and its order remain
preconditions: Table customers exists with primary key id and contains customers 1 and 2
Table orders exists with customer_id referencing customers.id ON DELETE CASCADE
Customer 1 has two orders (ids 101, 102); customer 2 has one order (id 201)
constraints: orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.id with ON DELETE CASCADE
Customer 2 and order 201 must remain unchanged after the test
setup_sql: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers;
CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, amount INTEGER NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customers (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Alice'), (2, 'Bob');
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount) VALUES (101, 1, 50), (102, 1, 75), (201, 2, 20);

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

expected_outcome.assertion_description: DELETE succeeds; customer 1 and its orders 101 and 102 are removed via cascade, leaving only customer 2 and order 201.

generated_test.title: Deleting customer with dependent order is rejected under ON DELETE RESTRICT
preconditions: Table customers exists with primary key column id and contains customer 1.

constraints: orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.id with ON DELETE RESTRICT.

setup_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT, amount INTEGER NOT NULL);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount) VALUES (100, 1, 250);

verification_assertions.query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;
SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

expected_outcome.assertion_description: The DELETE of customer 1 fails with a foreign key constraint violation because a dependent order exists and the FK uses ON DELETE RESTRICT; both the customer row and the order row remain unchanged.
